forms.en: I have made, I have done

at lave.explanation: "At lave" means "to make / do" for activities. "Hvad laver du?" means "What are you doing?", and "at lave mad" means "to cook". "At gøre" (to do) is used with a specific thing, as in "gøre noget ved det" (do something about it).

sentence.en: What are we going to do tonight?

at lave lektier.explanation: "At lave lektier" means "to do homework". Danish says "lave" (to make) where English says "do". You will often hear "Har du lavet dine lektier?" (Have you done your homework?).

sentence.en: The children do homework after school.

at lave mad.explanation: "At lave mad" means "to cook". It is made of "lave" (to make) and "mad" (food), so it literally means "to make food". "At koge" (to boil) is more specific. For any cooking, add the dish: "Jeg laver pasta" (I am making pasta).

sentence.en: My father cooks every day.

at le.explanation: "At le" means "to laugh": "Hun ler højt" (She laughs out loud) and "Vi lo meget" (We laughed a lot). "Latter" means "laughter".

sentence.en: We laughed all evening.

at lede efter.explanation: "At lede efter" means "to look for" something you cannot find yet: "Jeg leder efter mine nøgler" means "I am looking for my keys". Do not mix it up with "at se på" (to look at), which is for something you can already see.

sentence.en: I am looking for my keys.

at lege.explanation: "At lege" means "to play" the way children do, just for fun: "Børnene leger i haven" (The children are playing in the garden). For sports, games and instruments Danish uses "at spille" (to play).

sentence.en: The children are playing in the garden.

at leve.explanation: "At leve" means "to live (be alive)": "Hun lever stadig" (She is still alive). It is also used for how you live your life: "leve et godt liv" (to live a good life). For where your home is, Danes say "at bo" (to live somewhere). "Længe leve!" means "Long live!".

sentence.en: My grandfather is still alive.

at ligge.explanation: "At ligge" means "to lie (be lying)", to be lying down or placed flat: "Bogen ligger på bordet" (The book is lying on the table). It also says where places are: "Byen ligger ved havet" (The town is by the sea). Do not mix it up with "at lægge" (to put something down).

sentence.en: The book is lying on the table.

at like.explanation: "At like" means "to like (online)". It is borrowed straight from English and only means pressing "like" on a post. For liking a person, food or activity in real life, use "at kunne lide" (to like).

sentence.en: She usually likes my pictures.

at lukke.explanation: "At lukke" means "to close", for a door, a window, a shop or a bag. "Kan du lukke døren?" means "Can you close the door?". It is the opposite of "at åbne" (to open). In shops you may hear "Vi lukker om ti minutter" (We close in ten minutes).

sentence.en: Can you close the window, please?

at lytte.explanation: "At lytte" means "to listen" on purpose: "Jeg lytter til musik" (I am listening to music). It is used with "til" (to). "At høre" (to hear) is different: it is just noticing a sound, wanted or not. Compare "Jeg hørte en lyd" (I heard a sound) with "Jeg lyttede til musikken" (I listened to the music).

sentence.en: I listen to the radio in the morning.

at låne.explanation: "At låne" means "to borrow" and also "to lend", so the situation tells you which. "Kan jeg låne din pen?" means "Can I borrow your pen?". "Jeg låner dig min cykel" means "I lend you my bike". To be clear, Danes sometimes say "låne af" (borrow from) and "låne ud" (lend out).

sentence.en: Can I borrow your pen?

at lægge.explanation: "At lægge" means "to lay down": to put something down flat, like a book on a table or a baby in bed. "Jeg lægger bogen på bordet" means "I put the book on the table". Compare "at sætte" (to put something so it sits upright) and "at ligge" (to be lying somewhere). "Læg dig ned" means "Lie down".

sentence.en: She puts the book on the table.

at lære.explanation: "At lære" means "to learn" and also "to teach": "Jeg lærer dansk" (I learn Danish) and "Hun lærer mig dansk" (She teaches me Danish). "En lærer" (a teacher) looks just like "lærer" in "jeg lærer". Do not mix it up with "at læse" (to read).

sentence.en: I am learning Danish every day.

at læse.explanation: "At læse" means "to read": "Jeg læser en bog" (I am reading a book). It also means to study a subject at university: "Hun læser medicin" (She studies medicine). Do not mix it up with "at lære" (to learn).

sentence.en: I am reading a book in bed.

at løbe.explanation: "At løbe" means "to run", for sport or in a hurry: "Jeg løber hver morgen" (I run every morning). It is also used for a nose or a river that flows: "Min næse løber" (My nose is running). "At løbe tør for" means "to run out of".

sentence.en: I run in the park every morning.

en lampe.explanation: "En lampe" means "a lamp", such as a table lamp or a floor lamp. A ceiling light is "en loftlampe". "Tænd lampen" means "switch on the lamp", and "sluk lampen" means "switch off the lamp".

sentence.en: Can you switch on the lamp?

en landmand.explanation: "En landmand" means "a farmer", built from "land" (countryside) and "mand" (man). A farm is "en gård", and "landbrug" means "farming".

sentence.en: The farmer works in the field.

en lejlighed.explanation: "En lejlighed" means "an apartment" or "a flat". "At leje en lejlighed" means "to rent an apartment", while a whole house is "et hus". Size is often given in rooms: "en lejlighed med tre værelser" means "an apartment with three rooms".

sentence.en: We live in a small apartment.

en lillebror.explanation: "En lillebror" means "a little brother", meaning a brother who is younger than you. The older one is "en storebror" (a big brother).

sentence.en: My little brother goes to nursery school.

en lillesøster.explanation: "En lillesøster" means "a little sister", meaning a sister who is younger than you. The older one is "en storesøster" (a big sister).

sentence.en: My little sister loves to draw.

en liste.explanation: "En liste" means "a list", just like in English. Danes make "en indkøbsliste" (a shopping list) and "en huskeliste" (a reminder list). "At skrive noget på listen" means "to write something on the list".

sentence.en: I am writing a list.

en liter.explanation: "En liter" means "a liter". After a number it stays "liter": "to liter mælk" means "two liters of milk". Half a liter is "en halv liter".

sentence.en: I am buying two liters of milk.

en lomme.explanation: "En lomme" means "a pocket" on clothes: "Det er i min lomme" means "It is in my pocket". It is part of longer words like "lommepenge" (pocket money) and "en lommelygte" (a flashlight).

sentence.en: My keys are in my pocket.

en lufthavn.explanation: "En lufthavn" means "an airport". It is built from "luft" (air) and "havn" (harbour), so it is literally an "air harbour". "I lufthavnen" means "at the airport".

sentence.en: We are going to the airport at six o'clock.

en læbe.explanation: "En læbe" means "a lip". You will often use it for more than one: "røde læber" (red lips) or "tørre læber" (dry lips). Words like "læbestift" (lipstick) are built from it.

sentence.en: My lips are dry.

en læge.explanation: "En læge" means "a doctor", the person you see when you are ill. "At gå til lægen" means "to go to the doctor", and the word is the same for a man or a woman.

sentence.en: I am going to the doctor tomorrow.

en lærer.explanation: "En lærer" means "a teacher", for a man or a woman. "At lære" (to learn / to teach) is related: "en lærer" is the person who teaches.

sentence.en: Our teacher is very kind.

en løve.explanation: "En løve" means "a lion". The letter "ø" sounds a bit like the vowel in English "bird", said with rounded lips.

sentence.en: The lion roared loudly.

et land.explanation: "Et land" means "a country", and it can also mean "land" or "countryside". "På landet" means "in the countryside" and "i udlandet" means "abroad".

sentence.en: Denmark is a small country.

et liv.explanation: "Et liv" means "a life", both one person's life and life in general. Useful phrases are "livet er godt" (life is good) and "at have et godt liv" (to have a good life).

sentence.da: Jeg har et godt **liv** i Danmark.
sentence.en: I have a good life in Denmark.

et lår.explanation: "Et lår" means "a thigh", the top part of your leg between the hip and the knee. It is also used in cooking: "et kyllingelår" is a chicken thigh.

sentence.en: I have pain in my thigh.

et løg.explanation: "Et løg" means "an onion". Danes use "løg" a lot in cooking, and "ristede løg" (fried onions) are a classic topping on a hot dog.

sentence.en: I am cutting an onion.

forms.da: Lad os se, hvad klokken er.
forms.en: Let's see what time it is.

forms.da: Lad os se, om han kommer.

lad os se.explanation: "Lad os se" means "let's see", and you say it while you think, check something or wait for a result. "Lad" works like "let", so "lad os gå" (let's go) is built the same way.

sentence.da: **Lad os se**, hvad der er i køleskabet.
sentence.en: Let's see what is in the fridge.

laks.explanation: "Laks" means "salmon", the fish. When you talk about it as food you do not put "en" in front: "Jeg spiser laks" (I eat salmon).

sentence.en: I eat salmon with potatoes.

lang.explanation: "Lang" means "long", in distance or in time. "Langt" on its own also means "far": "Det er langt væk" (It is far away). The opposite is "kort" (short), and "længere" means "longer".

sentence.en: It is a long day.

langsom.explanation: "Langsom" means "slow". To say that something happens slowly, use "langsomt": "Tal langsomt, tak" (Speak slowly, please). The opposite is "hurtig" (fast).

sentence.en: Can you speak a little more slowly?

forms.en: The hotel is far from the town.

langt fra.explanation: "Langt fra" means "far from", followed by the place you mean. It is the opposite of "tæt på" (close to). On its own, "langt fra" can also mean "far from it", a way to say "not at all".

sentence.en: Our house is far from the town.

langt væk.explanation: "Langt væk" means "far away". "Langt" means "far" or "long" and "væk" means "away". You use it for something a great distance from you. The opposite idea is "tæt på" (close to) or "i nærheden" (nearby).

sentence.en: My family lives far away.

lav.explanation: "Lav" means "low", and it is also used for a person who is short. It works for prices too: "lave priser" means "low prices". The opposite is "høj" (tall, high), and "lavere" means "lower".

sentence.en: The price is very low.

legetøj.explanation: "Legetøj" means "toys", all of them as a group, and it stays the same for one or many. "Mit legetøj" means "my toys". For one toy, say "et stykke legetøj" (a piece of toys) or name it, like "en bamse" (a teddy bear).

sentence.en: The children have a lot of toys.

lektier.explanation: "Lektier" means "homework". It is always said in the "more than one" form, so "mange lektier" means "a lot of homework". The usual word for doing it is "at lave" (to do, to make): "Jeg laver lektier" (I do my homework). "En lektie" is one piece of homework, but it is rarely used.

sentence.en: I have a lot of homework today.

let.explanation: "Let" means "easy" or "light in weight": "en let opgave" (an easy task) and "en let taske" (a light bag). The situation shows which one you mean. The opposite of easy is "svær" (difficult), and of light it is "tung" (heavy). Another everyday word for easy is "nem".

sentence.en: Danish is not that easy.

lidt.explanation: "Lidt" means "a little" or "a bit", for amounts and for degrees, as in "lidt mælk" (a little milk) and "lidt træt" (a bit tired). Do not mix it up with "lille" (small), which says how big something is. The opposite of "lidt" is "meget" (a lot).

sentence.en: I speak a little Danish.

forms.en: Can you speak a bit slower?

lidt langsommere, tak.explanation: "Lidt langsommere, tak" means "a bit slower, please", and a learner says it when Danish is spoken too fast. "Langsommere" means "slower" (from "langsom", slow). To ask for it to be repeated too, add "Kan du sige det igen?" (Can you say that again?).

sentence.da: Jeg er ny i Danmark. **Lidt langsommere, tak.**
sentence.en: I am new in Denmark. A bit slower, please.

lige.explanation: "Lige" means "straight" or "equal", and in "et lige tal" it means "even" (2, 4, 6). It is also a very common little word meaning "just" or "right": "lige nu" is "right now" and "lige ved siden af" is "right next to". The opposite of straight is "skæv" (crooked).

sentence.en: The street is straight.

forms.en: What are you doing right now?

lige nu.explanation: "Lige nu" means "right now", at this very moment. "Nu" means "now" and "lige" means "just", which makes it more exact. For something a little later, use "om lidt" (in a little while).

sentence.en: I do not have time right now.

forms.en: He is just like his father.

ligesom.explanation: "Ligesom" means "just like" or "the same as", and you use it to compare two things that are alike: "Du er ligesom din mor" (You are just like your mother). It is stronger than "som" (like, as), because "lige" means "exactly".

sentence.en: You are just like your father.

lilla.explanation: "Lilla" means "purple", and in everyday speech it also covers lilac and violet shades. Unlike many colour words it never gets an ending, so it stays "lilla" even in "et lilla tørklæde".

sentence.en: I have a purple bag.

lille.explanation: "Lille" means "small" or "little", and it is also used for children: "en lille dreng" means "a little boy". "Mindre" means "smaller", and the opposite of "lille" is "stor" (big).

sentence.en: We have a small apartment.

luft.explanation: "Luft" means "air". "I luften" means "in the air", and "frisk luft" (fresh air) is a common phrase. It is also the first part of "en lufthavn" (an airport), which is literally an "air harbour".

sentence.en: I need some fresh air.

lukket.explanation: "Lukket" means "closed", for doors, shops, windows and roads. It is the opposite of "åben" (open). You will see "Lukket" on shop doors when the shop is shut. "At lukke" means "to close".

sentence.en: The bank is closed today.

lys.explanation: "Lys" means "light" or "bright", for light colours and for rooms or days full of daylight. The opposite is "mørk" (dark). There is also a different word "et lys", which means "a candle" or "a light".

sentence.en: The kitchen is very bright in the morning.

lyseblå.explanation: "Lyseblå" means "light blue". It is "lys" (light) and "blå" (blue) joined into one word. The darker one is "mørkeblå" (dark blue).

sentence.en: She has a light blue shirt.

lysegrøn.explanation: "Lysegrøn" means "light green". It is "lys" (light) and "grøn" (green) joined into one word. The darker one is "mørkegrøn" (dark green).

sentence.en: She has a light green dress.

lyserød.explanation: "Lyserød" means "pink". It is "lys" (light) and "rød" (red) joined into one word, so it is literally "light red".

sentence.en: The child has a pink sweater.

lækker.explanation: "Lækker" means "delicious" or "tasty", and Danes use it often to praise food. It can also mean "nice-looking", so "en lækker bil" is "a great-looking car", and it is used for more than food.

sentence.en: The soup is really delicious.

længe.explanation: "Længe" means "for a long time": "Jeg har ventet længe" (I have waited a long time). "For længe siden" means "a long time ago". Do not mix it up with "lang" (long), which says how long something is: "en lang vej" (a long road).

sentence.en: I have lived here for a long time.

lørdag.explanation: "En lørdag" means "a Saturday". "På lørdag" means "this coming Saturday", and "om lørdagen" means "on Saturdays" (every Saturday). Day names start with a small letter in Danish.

sentence.en: We do the shopping on Saturdays.
